comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C2, C26-C28, C57. Both evaluations support the finding that atomoxetine and cue validity enhance drift rate in the DDM. OpenEval provides detailed statistical support (p<0.001 for cue validity, p=0.02 for ATX), while peer reviewers explicitly affirm these as 'solid evidence' with 'overlapping effects on performance.'

Perfect agreement on claims C67-C69. Both evaluations support the CPP characterization findings showing differential relationships with accuracy vs. speed and correlation with drift rate. OpenEval provides detailed analysis, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings through their statement about 'meticulously reported' results using 'state-of-the art EEG methods.'

Perfect agreement on claim C55. Both evaluations support the drug × cue interaction on EDAN component. OpenEval notes the finding is statistically supported (p=0.01) but acknowledges interpretive caution about EDAN's functional significance. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through their statement that 'EEG findings provide solid evidence' for interactive effects.

Strong agreement on claims C48-C50, C53, C56, C59 regarding alpha power findings. Both evaluations support the distinct spatial profiles of attention (lateralization) vs. neuromodulation (bilateral suppression). OpenEval provides detailed statistics (p<0.001 for attention, p=0.003 for ATX), while peer reviewers explicitly note 'distinct effects on EEG signatures of pre-stimulus cortical excitability.'

Strong agreement on claims C39, C42, C44, C58 regarding temporal dissociation of attention and drug effects on stimulus-locked ERPs. Both evaluations support the finding that attention modulated early activity (70-336 ms) while drug effects emerged later (406-586 ms). OpenEval provides detailed statistics, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'dissociable effects on corresponding EEG markers.'

Agreement on claim C29 regarding ATX increasing non-decision time. OpenEval provides detailed statistical support (p=0.048) and explicitly evaluates this claim. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through their statement that results are 'meticulously reported' with 'state-of-the art modeling.'

Agreement on claims C30-C31 regarding null effects on boundary separation and drift rate variability. Both evaluations support these null findings. OpenEval explicitly evaluates them as part of the DDM results, while peer reviewers implicitly accept them through their endorsement of the 'meticulously reported' modeling results.

Agreement on claims C61-C62 regarding the drift rate interaction and lack of CPP interaction. Both evaluations support these findings. OpenEval notes the drift rate interaction is statistically supported but small (effect size 0.04) and urges caution. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'interactive' effects between attention and neuromodulation.

Partial overlap on claims C4, C63 regarding overall patterns of main effects and interactions. Both evaluations support the overarching conclusions. OpenEval provides detailed evaluation of specific claims, while peer reviewers strongly endorse the overall conclusion as 'solid evidence' about how attention and neuromodulation jointly shape decision-making.

Agreement on claim C65 regarding the null replication of drug × cue interaction on alpha lateralization. Both evaluations support this null finding. OpenEval notes the failure to replicate is appropriately acknowledged with possible explanations, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this through their statement that 'more work is necessary to determine the effects of cholinergic neuromodulation.'

Agreement on claims C71-C72 regarding weaker and sometimes opposite effects of donepezil compared to atomoxetine. OpenEval rates these claims as UNCERTAIN due to speculative mechanistic explanations, while peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge this pattern and fairly note that 'more work is necessary to determine the effects of cholinergic neuromodulation.'

Agreement on claim C21 regarding blinding limitations. Both evaluations support this methodological acknowledgment. OpenEval includes it as part of the pharmacological validation claims, noting it is 'appropriately acknowledged.' Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through their description of the study as 'meticulously reported.'

OpenEval result R9 evaluates claim C60 as a summary inference about temporal and spatial dissociation between attention and neuromodulation effects. No corresponding standalone peer review result found, though peer reviewers support related claims about dissociable effects in other results (R4, R5).

OpenEval result R12 evaluates claim C66 regarding the methodological limitation of anti-correlation between tonic and phasic neuromodulation. No corresponding peer review result found addressing this specific limitation.

OpenEval result R13 evaluates claim C54 regarding alpha lateralization predicting behavioral benefits without drug modulation. No corresponding peer review result found specifically addressing this analysis.

OpenEval result R14 evaluates claims C77-C79 regarding standard methodological and ethical procedures. No corresponding peer review result found, as peer reviewers did not comment on these procedural aspects.

OpenEval result R1 evaluates claims C15-C16, C19, C21, C80-C83 regarding pharmacological manipulation and physiological validation. While peer review R12 addresses C21 and R9 addresses C19, no peer review result comprehensively evaluates this full set of pharmacological validation claims.
